items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS so unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG) ends a request at a usage limit that resets too far away instead of waiting
  • Added OpenTelemetry tracing guidance to the claude-api skill, including setting up trace destinations with the ant CLI
  • Added the % motion to vim mode: jump to the matching bracket, alone or with d/c/y
  • Added rows to a mod's Input: a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter submits and Shift+Enter or a backslash before Enter starts a new line
  • Added classifier_verdict and permission_mode to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, so auto mode classifier decisions can be told apart from permission rules
  • Added classifier_category to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, naming the built-in rule a classifier block matched, when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1
  • Fixed quitting removing a worktree made by a WorktreeCreate hook without asking when it may hold unpushed commits
  • Fixed the fable (and best) model alias erroring on the Anthropic API when the newest Fable model is not available to your organization: Claude Code now retries once on the previous Fable model
  • Fixed a misleading "Please run /login" error when a full disk keeps the login from being refreshed; the error now names the disk and says to delete files
  • Fixed Grep and Glob reporting no matches when the search program failed unexpectedly before returning any results; they now return an error saying the search failed
  • Fixed workflow agents sometimes skipping their step, and the run still reporting success, after reading the harness note that their task text carries no user authority
  • Fixed artifact updates being refused where a PreToolUse hook covers Edit or Write; Claude now edits the file and then republishes instead of changing it in the publish call
  • Fixed skills and commands with very many or very long argument names stalling for seconds when invoked; only the first 64 names, each up to 64 characters, are now filled in
  • Fixed skills, commands and hooks using very large amounts of memory when their arguments fill many placeholders
  • Fixed stray characters such as >0q covering the folder trust prompt, and >4m before the shell prompt at exit, in terminals built on VTE older than 0.53 such as MATE Terminal on RHEL 8
  • Fixed stray GOK text appearing in the prompt at startup in some versions of iTerm2
  • Fixed switching to a model whose name contains application-inference-profile running your awsAuthRefresh command and delaying model-switch hooks when the provider is not Bedrock
  • Fixed sign-in refresh timeouts and unexpected sign-outs after a short command such as claude auth status or claude plugin list exited in the middle of a token refresh
  • Fixed a tool call cut off by a message sent mid-turn during its permission check being reported to the model as rejected by the user
  • Fixed a case where switching to a model with a smaller context window could spend usage credits on a summary by the previous model without asking first
  • Fixed conversations being compacted over and over, on a model you didn't pick, behind an LLM gateway whose responses name a different model than the one requested
  • Fixed vim mode sometimes staying in INSERT after Escape on a slow or busy machine
  • Fixed Esc discarding a typed AskUserQuestion answer in vim mode: the free-text field now supports vim NORMAL mode, and Esc cancels only from NORMAL
  • Fixed the Read tool reading binary files such as .xlsm, .parquet, .epub and .heic as text
  • Fixed a Markdown table with only a header row drawing nothing when too wide for the terminal, including in plans on the plan approval card
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying CMEK external-key endpoints aren't available on Claude Platform on AWS
  • Fixed skills no longer being listed to the model after using /rewind
  • Fixed the compaction row in a resumed session offering ctrl+o for history that is not loaded; it now says where the earlier messages are saved, and also shows in fullscreen
  • Fixed the "new task? /clear to save tokens" hint coming back right after you interrupt a response
  • Fixed the permission prompt for a plugin or skill hook's ask decision not showing which plugin or skill the hook comes from
  • Fixed /diff not noticing a conflicted cherry-pick or revert in reftable repositories when one of its git checks timed out or failed
  • Fixed workflow scripts asking for permission or being refused when read, edited or re-run after a Bash cd in the same session
  • Fixed dim text on the dark ANSI theme and 16-color terminals: faint inside filled boxes, not faint under selection and search highlights, and list descriptions dimmed like other secondary text
  • Fixed a mod's $.model.fork returning nothing-to-fork when called before the first response of a new Claude Code process had finished, as in claude -p runs and cloud sessions
  • Fullscreen mode: Fixed /compact and auto-compact briefly freezing the UI while the visible transcript is rebuilt
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions started from Slack being unable to find or attach a repository when managed settings restrict MCP servers; use deniedMcpServers to keep those tools off
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions being reported as having a deleted source branch, and not retried, when an unrelated setup or session failure quoted git's missing-ref wording
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed the log promising a retry of a failed or declined session release for a session that is ending; repeated failures now show a count
  • Windows: Fixed stopped background PowerShell commands missing the closing [killed] line in their output file
  • Improved switching to a model with a smaller context window: a conversation too long for the new model is now summarized by the previous model first
  • Improved rendering performance while a long-running subagent works: its progress trail now updates incrementally instead of being reprocessed in full on every render
  • Improved artifacts: pages Claude writes now paint the band above a sticky header, so scrolled text no longer shows there in the mobile apps
  • Improved mods: in VS Code and the desktop and mobile apps, a tree drawn above the question dialog can now hold Markdown and up to 48 rows; the terminal keeps 12 plain rows
  • Changed a mod hook's .catch handler to run only when the hook throws or times out; events raised beneath the hook's own calls now skip that hook without asking its .catch
  • Changed a mod's $.env.set to resolve with {} once the variable is set or unset, or with { deny } saying why when the write is not made
  • [VSCode] Added LaTeX math rendering in Claude's responses, including $$ and multi-line \[ … \] blocks and inline $…$ and \(…\) math
  • [VSCode] Added a "Get more usage" link to the usage-limit banner for Pro and Max plans in the VS Code and JetBrains panels
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation that crashes or freezes the panel being reopened on every reload
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down during long thinking: it no longer re-parses the whole thinking text on every update
  • [VSCode] Fixed diagnostics showing "[object Object]" instead of the rule code (e.g. MD013) for some language servers
  • [VSCode] Fixed the native dictation audio module being loaded, to check microphone permission, where dictation is not offered (non-claude.ai sign-ins, remote windows)

items.content:
• Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups.
  • To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle.
  • We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t.

Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type.

That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. 

From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop

Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step.

With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it.

With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration.

When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t.

So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change.

With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible:

Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike.

Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers.

Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. 

Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action.  

The Operating Model

That ownership model needs machinery with five key components:

  • Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone.
  • Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke.
  • Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. 
  • Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review.
  • Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created.

Adapting the Environment to the Models

The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. 

Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. 

Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from.

Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. 

This gave us three things at once: 

  • Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. 
  • Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. 
  • No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. 

The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect.

Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing

Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause.

One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions.

While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness.

Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed

We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places:

Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself.

Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. 

What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it.

Did It Work?

Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile:

  • Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults.
  • Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality.
  • Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. 

The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework.

What Worked, and What Did Not

Acknowledgements 

We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions.

items.title: The Most Common Questions About Agent Evals, Answered
items.summary:
• Evals score your agent's runs so you can check that it behaves the way you expect. To get started, pick one behavior, build a small dataset from real traces, and run a baseline. Use offline evals before you ship and online evals in production, and turn new failures into dataset examples.
  • Use code evaluators where you can, LLM judges where you can't, and human review to check both. For agents that take many steps, evaluate full threads, trajectories, and final state.
  • Benchmarks like Terminal-Bench are offline evals with longer tasks and their own environments. Harbor runs them and logs the results to LangSmith experiments.

As you build and ship an agent, you’ll need a way to check that it behaves the way you expect, both in development and once real users start relying on it.

In traditional software, the same inputs produce the same outputs, so a unit test can check for an exact result. Agents are harder to test for a few reasons:

  • Outputs vary between runs, even for the same request
  • More than one answer can be correct, so checking for an exact match falls short
  • The agent chooses its own steps, so a correct output can still come from a “wrong” path. For example, an agent might call a tool it doesn't need or take an action without user permission.

Agent evals are the solution. They score your agent’s runs with checks that account for these variations. Similar to the agents they evaluate, these tests are not one-size-fits-all, and the best suite of evals depends on the team, their product, and what they want to optimize for.

Over the past few years of working on LangSmith, LangChain’s platform for agent engineering, our team has encountered a lot of different eval questions. This blog walks through some of the most common questions on how to get started with agent evals and the different types of evals you can use in your workflows.

Where should we start?

Every eval starts with understanding what your agent actually does. A trace is a record of one run of your agent, including its inputs, outputs, and every model and tool call in between. Read through a sample of its traces to see how it handles requests and where it goes wrong. What you find tells you what to test first. Start small.

  1. Pick a behavior you care about. For example, for a travel assistant, a behavior could be whether it books the date and price range the user asked for.
  2. Build a small dataset from traces. A dataset is a collection of examples, and each example is a single test case with an input and often an expected output. Ten to twenty examples of a behavior is enough to start, and in LangSmith you can add traces to a dataset straight from the tracing view. If your agent isn't in production yet, have your team or a small group of trusted design partners test it out (dogfooding) and work from those traces.
  3. Run a baseline. Run your current agent against the dataset and save the result as an experiment. An experiment contains the results of running one version of your agent on a dataset, along with the scores from your evaluators. You’ll compare the performance of future versions of your agent with this experiment.
  4. Add new failures as you find them. Each failure you see in production or while testing becomes a new example.

Continue adding failures to your dataset and you have an improvement loop. Find a failure, add it to your dataset, improve the agent, and rerun. As you identify more agent behaviors to evaluate, you'll expand your eval suite following the same pattern as above.

What's the difference between offline and online evals?

Evals can and should run before you ship a change and after your agent is live. Before shipping, evals can tell you whether a change made the agent better or worse. After shipping, evals can tell you how the agent is performing with real users.

Offline evals run your agent against a dataset before you ship a change. You choose the example inputs, and you can also include expected outputs (also called reference outputs). Using your dataset, you can compare experiment results across agent versions. They’re best used to test a new prompt, model, or tool, and to catch regressions before they reach users.

Benchmarks like Terminal-Bench are also offline evals, built on a fixed set of tasks so you can compare agents, models, or versions. Harbor runs them and logs the results to LangSmith experiments, which we cover in more detail below.

Online evals score real production traces as they come in. There's usually no reference output to compare against, so they rely on code checks and LLM judges that can grade a run on its own. They’re best used to monitor quality and find the problems your dataset missed.

You need both, and they feed into each other. Failures that online evals flag become new examples in your offline dataset.

There are a few ways to build a dataset for offline evals in LangSmith. You can write examples from scratch, add runs from your existing traces, send over runs your team reviewed in an annotation queue, upload a CSV or JSONL file, or generate synthetic examples from a few you already have.

As your eval suite grows, you'll need to decide whether to add examples to an existing dataset or start a new one. As a rule of thumb:

  • Keep examples in the same dataset when they test the same behavior with the same evaluators, so experiments stay comparable over time.
  • Create a new dataset when the inputs look different (like single requests vs full conversations), when you need different evaluators, or when the dataset serves a different purpose, like a small set that runs on every pull request vs a larger one you run before a release.

Within a single dataset, you can also use splits to run a subset of examples.

What are the different types of agent evaluators?

An evaluator is the logic that scores a run. There are four common types. Most teams start with one or two and add more over time.

  • Code evaluators check things deterministically, like whether the booked price is under the user's budget. They're fast, cheap, and consistent, though their need for deterministic inputs and outputs limit their usefulness.
  • LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to grade things code can't, like whether the assistant's reply clearly confirms the flight details.
  • Human review has your team or subject matter experts score runs directly. It's slower, but it's the best signal for subjective quality and for checking your other evaluators. It’s often used on a smaller sample to then inform an LLM evaluator’s judgement.
  • Pairwise evaluators compare two outputs side by side and pick the better one, which is useful when you're choosing between two prompts or models.

Any of these evaluators can be pointed at different parts of an agent’s run. An eval might score:

  • A single step. Ex. Whether search_flights was called with the right date.
  • The final response. Ex. Whether the reply confirms the flight the agent actually booked.
  • A full conversation. Ex. Whether the final booking reflects every change the user asked for across several turns
  • The end state of an environment. Ex. The booking records in a mock booking system after the agent runs in its own container. Benchmarks often use this setup, and you’ll sometimes hear these called containerized evals.

Can you trust an LLM judge?

An LLM judge uses a model to grade outputs that are difficult to check with code, like whether an answer is supported by the retrieved documents. Judges are flexible, but they can be inconsistent and drift from your team's judgement. A few habits make them reliable:

  • Compare the judge with human scores. Have someone on your team grade a sample of runs and check where the judge disagrees. Adjust the judge's prompt or examples until they line up. Annotation queues in LangSmith make this easy. Our LLM-as-a-judge docs walk you through this.
  • Ask narrow questions. In our travel agent example, asking "Does the reply mention every layover?" is easier to judge than "Is this a good reply?"
  • Define a precise scoring scale. A binary pass or fail, or a small set of labeled categories, is far more reproducible than scoring on a 1-10 scale. A judge may have a hard time distinguishing between a score of 6 vs 7.

Are evals the same as benchmarks?

A benchmark is a type of offline eval composed of a set of tasks. A task is a single test case in a benchmark, including instructions, an environment in a container, and a test script that scores the result. As agents become more capable, a simple LLM judge or code-based eval often isn't enough. Agents can now execute code, edit files, and interface with services. To model this multi-step behavior, benchmarks set up isolated infrastructure in containers. This lets developers test agent behavior offline the same way the agent will work in production.

Benchmarks differ from simpler LLM judges and code-based evals in a few ways:

  • Tasks involve more steps. To complete a single task, an agent might install packages, edit files, and run commands across dozens of tool calls.
  • Each task comes with an environment. Agents can now take actions in environments like a sandbox with a code repo, files, and tools. Every task ships with its own isolated environment for the agent to work in.
  • Scoring checks what the agent did. A test script inspects the state of the environment after the run, like whether the tests pass or the right file exists. You can still review the trace, but the score comes from the actions the agent took and the state it left behind.

For our travel assistant, a benchmark task might give the agent a mock booking system and a request such as "A storm canceled the traveler's flight to Denver. Rebook them and move their hotel to match." Once the agent finishes, the test script would check the booking records in the database.

Harbor is an open source eval harness that provides the scaffolding for testing on these longer tasks. It's the framework that powers Terminal-Bench, and you can use the same task format to build a benchmark for your own agent. With the LangSmith integration, each Harbor run is logged as a LangSmith experiment. Harbor builds a container for each task, and you can use LangSmith traces to make each environment closer to what your agent sees in production. Benchmark results then sit alongside the rest of your evals, and you can open any run to see the full trace next to its score.

We used this setup to improve Deep Agents on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by reviewing traces to find failure modes and then changing the harness. We also used it to build IssueBench, a benchmark for LangSmith Engine. Each IssueBench task gives Engine a batch of traces and scores whether it groups the correct ones into the right issue clusters.

Building a benchmark for your own agent follows the same steps as the evals above, with a few changes:

  • Collect tasks from traces. Find failures in LangSmith traces, then turn each one into a Harbor task with its own environment, like a mock booking system populated with a user’s reservations.
  • Define what “good” looks like. Create LLM judges or code-based evals that score based on your rubric.
  • Hill climb on the score. Run the agent and use the scores to A/B test changes. You can set up an agent loop that runs through this process for you. It would make edits to your agent, rerun the benchmark, and keep or revert each change, similar to Andrej Karpathy’s autoresearch loop from a few months ago.

How can you evaluate production traffic without high costs?

Offline evals run on a fixed dataset, so their cost is predictable. Online evals run on live traffic, so if an LLM judge scores every trace, your eval costs grow with every new user. To keep them affordable:

  • Sample and filter. Online evaluators in LangSmith can score a percentage of traffic, or only traces that match a filter like negative user feedback.
  • Use code checks where you can. Checking whether the booking matches the requested date, or whether the agent searched before booking, costs almost nothing.
  • Use a cheaper judge. In our Jev-as-a-Judge experiment, Jev from TypeSafe AI matched human labels on every pass/fail decision and cost $0.34 in total, compared with $28.17 for Claude Sonnet 4.6.

Online eval costs are saved over time in LangSmith, so teams can monitor their spending.

Do you have to build your own agent evals?

No, especially when you’re evaluating for common agent issues. A good place to start is with our prebuilt LLM evaluator templates in LangSmith for typical checks like hallucination or PII leakage. Add one to a dataset or tracing project and edit its prompt to fit your agent, like telling the judge our travel assistant should never book outside the user's budget.

Our open source agentevals package also has prebuilt evaluators for an agent's messages and tool calls. They can compare the tools your agent called against a reference list, or ask an LLM judge whether the steps made sense.

You can also reuse an offline evaluator across datasets and run it as an online evaluator on production traces (only works if the evaluator does not require a reference output).

For evals specific to your agent, the Eval Engineering Skill runs in coding agents like Claude Code or Codex, reads your repo and traces, and writes runnable evals with you.

LangSmith Engine can also write evals for you automatically by pulling from production traces. When it identifies an issue cluster, it turns the failing traces into dataset examples and writes their reference outputs as assertions, such as “Books a flight on the date the user requested.”

How do you evaluate multi-turn conversations?

Many agents work across several turns. For example, a user might ask our travel assistant for flights, change the date, then add a hotel. Each turn can look fine on its own while the conversation as a whole goes wrong.

To evaluate conversations in LangSmith, pass a thread ID in your trace metadata so each turn is grouped into a thread. A thread is a sequence of traces from the same conversation. From there you can attach online evaluators that score a whole thread once the conversation ends, with questions like "Did the final booking reflect every change the user asked for?" or "Did the user have to repeat themselves?" LangSmith also shows each thread as a trajectory, with every message and tool call listed once, in order.

For offline evals, you can store full conversations as examples in a dataset, or simulate the user with an LLM so you can test how the agent handles a conversation from start to finish.

How do you evaluate an agent beyond its final output?

Agents take many steps, so the final answer only shows part of what happened. Beyond the final response, you may want to check:

  • The path, meaning the sequence of messages and tool calls the agent produced.
  • The final state, such as the booking record our travel agent created, a file it wrote, or a change it made to a repo.

As your production agents become increasingly more complex, you may need a dedicated eval harness. Specifically, when the agent's work is the change it makes to an environment. Say a coding agent is asked to fix a bug. An LLM judge can read the agent's reply, but the reliable check is to run the repo's tests after the agent finishes. For that to work, every test run needs its own clean copy of the repo so runs don't affect each other. Harbor sets this up for you. You can run agents built with Deep Agents in LangSmith Sandboxes and log each run, along with its trace, to a LangSmith experiment. Learn more in Harbor x LangChain.

Can you trace and evaluate an agent in LangSmith if it's not built using LangChain, LangGraph, or Deep Agents?

Yes! LangSmith is framework agnostic, so you can trace and evaluate an agent built with any framework, or with no framework at all. There are a few ways to send traces:

  • Framework integrations. LangSmith has integrations for popular agent frameworks like the OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, and more.
  • Model provider wrappers. If you call a model provider directly, wrap the client for OpenAI or Anthropic and each model call is traced.
  • The @traceable decorator. Add it to your own functions, like the travel assistant's flight search tool, to trace any step of your agent.

Once your traces are in LangSmith, evals work the same way for any framework. You can add traces to a dataset, run offline experiments by passing your agent to the SDK’s evaluate() function, and attach online evaluators to production traffic.

How do you move off an existing eval stack?

You don't have to start over. Most of what you've already built carries over to LangSmith:

  • Datasets. Upload existing test cases as a CSV or JSONL file, or create them with the SDK.
  • Code evaluators. Existing scoring functions usually need only small changes to run as LangSmith evaluators. If your evals already run as tests, the pytest and Vitest integrations let you keep that setup.
  • LLM judges. Paste your existing judge prompt into an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator in the UI, or keep it in code.
  • Tracing. LangSmith works with any framework, so you can send traces from your current agent without rewriting it.

How do you report results?

Offline experiments show whether each release improved. Online eval dashboards show how performance holds up in production over time. In LangSmith, you can directly compare experiment results and create custom dashboards for metrics such as token cost, latency, and evaluator scores over time. A benchmark gives you a stable score to compare models or agent versions across releases.

Next

If you want to go deeper, read How We Build Evals for Deep Agents, try the LangSmith evaluation quickstart, or check out our LangChain Academy course on LangSmith Essentials.

Prefer a live instructor? I’ll be hosting a virtual workshop on agent evals on October 28, 2026. Register here!

items.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
items.summary:
Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial [...]

Read More...

The post 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record!

There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. 

Some highlights:

  • WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second.
  • Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak.
  • Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. 
  • Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline.
  • Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6.
  • Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup.

Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball 

Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. 

But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament.

It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. 

Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern.

Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention

Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand.

Region-Specific Capacity

Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament.

Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges

For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience.

During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours.


Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final.

  1. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament.
  2. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality.
  3. Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems.
  4. Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after.

All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics.

WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes

Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption.

That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed.

Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t.

We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms.

We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. 

We Stay Ready Year-Round

Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one.

Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.

items.title: Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award
items.summary:
Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went [...]

Read More...

The post Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta.

Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes.

Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality.

Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp. 

We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true.

As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start.

The post Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.summary:
Zero-knowledge proofs can verify computing results without rerunning workloads or exposing sensitive data. Magnetar helps bring them into the mainstream with support for standard programming languages, major speed gains, and quantum-resistant security.

The post Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • A new form of computing. Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run.
  • Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption: making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now.
  • Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical.

A new form of computing

Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. 

Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private.

This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program.

Three grand challenges

Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time.

Efficiency. Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere.

Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. 

Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029. Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. 

PODCAST SERIES

Ideas

Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets.

Listen now
Opens in a new tab

More than a decade of work

For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab)lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab), but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab)used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers.

In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: 

  • Phalanx (opens in new tab), in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea.  
  • Nova (opens in new tab), HyperNova (opens in new tab), NeutronNova (opens in new tab), Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost.
  • Brakedown (opens in new tab), in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. 
  • Spice (opens in new tab), Lasso (opens in new tab), Nebula (opens in new tab), and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor.
  • Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second.
  • More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab), a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab), which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. 

Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together.

Magnetar

Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once.

It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. 

It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. 

Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. 

The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain.

The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements.

Looking ahead

Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust.

If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab).

Opens in a new tab

The post Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.title: Open From Data Center to Desktop: NVIDIA Expands Nemotron Family With Highest Efficiency Super VL and Bolt Models
items.summary: NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents. Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized […]
items.content:
NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents.

Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents.

Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23.

The three open models together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware. 

Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability. 

Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside Lightning and Ultra. 

Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge. 

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: Frontier Accuracy at One-Fifth the Size

Super VL, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition, delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.

As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks. 

Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Agentic Intelligence at the Edge

Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications.

Relative to other models with a similar memory footprint, it provides a good balance of intelligence and speed: smart enough to get most jobs done, yet much faster than the smartest models.

 

With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on PinchBench, and the #2 open model for BrowseComp.

Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. 

Adoption of Custom Super Intelligence

Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments. 

Super VL is being post-trained and customized by organizations across industries. Scale AI post-trained the model for Skydance’s vendor credit finance agent and for EY’s M&A due diligence agent. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. AI21 and Alice post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. ModelScope enables developers to fine-tune the model through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications.

Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream, sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and R1 for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions.

Software platform companies integrating Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include: 

  • Atlassian, for tasks like agentic search across apps such as Jira and Confluence.
  • CrowdStrike, which is customizing the model for agentic blue teaming in enterprise security.
  • Dassault Systèmes, powering engineering design and simulation. 
  • Perplexity, for search and agentic tasks in Perplexity Search and Computer.
  • Salesforce, which is customizing Nemotron to power AI agents that digitize and automate complex government workflows in secure customer environments through Missionforce Operations.
  • Synopsys software for semiconductor design verification interoperates with the model.

What Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Actually Sees

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s vision language strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents. 

It processes a web page, extracts text, reads graphs and charts, and returns insights from what it finds. The same applies to PDFs and other documents agents commonly work with.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision. 

Open for Maximum Control, Security, and Privacy

Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes.

Control runs in two directions. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions.

In insurance, for example, a customized agent can scan claims for fraud markers on repeat. In financial services, an agent can review credit scores and flag activity against an organization’s own lending criteria. The model stays on premises. The data stays private.

Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was trained on about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining, then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments.

NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use, finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym.

NVIDIA NIM packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements.

And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, ModelScope community and as NVIDIA NIM.

Runs on DGX Spark, DGX Station, and RTX 

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on DGX Spark, DGX Station,  RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on NVIDIA Jetson at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, and vLLM. Built for NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on GeForce RTX PCs, DGX Spark, DGX Station and RTX PRO workstations.

Download the open weights, explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the technical blog for the full architecture breakdown.

Stay up to date on agents, NVIDIA Nemotron and more by subscribing to NVIDIA news, joining the community, and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn, Instagram, X and Facebook.

Explore self-paced video tutorials and livestreams.

Then, step into the Shroud as Keen Games’ Enshrouded leaves early access with its 1.0 release, or let the bolts fly in Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2. Both are streaming on GeForce NOW at launch.

With 10 new games joining the cloud this week, members can put the new controls to work in supported titles and keep playing across supported devices without downloads, installs or expensive hardware upgrades.

Fine-Tune the Cloud With DLSS 4.5 Controls

NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls are now available on GeForce NOW, giving members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware. DLSS Super Resolution sharpens image quality, while Dynamic Multi Frame Generation delivers lower latency and reduces stutter for smoother streaming, and Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced visuals. In addition, Ultimate members streaming on GeForce RTX 5080-powered cloud rigs benefit from the maximum available options, including Dynamic Multi Frame Generation up to 4X.  

From James Bond’s globe-trotting missions in 007 First Light — now with path tracing support — to CONTROL Resonant’s reality-bending Manhattan and the shadowy scares of Resident Evil Requiem, the controls help fine-tune supported games for image quality, responsiveness or a preferred balance between the two.

These new settings are available in the GeForce NOW app under settings, for Windows, macOS, Chrome OS and Steam OS platforms. Members can read here for more details on using the feature with their membership tier, and more information on how to get the smoothest cloud game streaming for some games on GeForce NOW.

Rise, Flameborn

Enshrouded 1.0 brings the co-op survival action role-playing game out of early access and into its full release. Rise as a Flameborn, the last ember of hope of a dying race, and venture into a vast world of survival, action and role-playing, where a corrupting fog has consumed a once-beautiful kingdom.

The title brings improvements to existing systems, alongside expansions in combat with nine new spells, new mage and archer skills, reworked wands and upgradeable Eternal spells and arrows. New enemy variants keep encounters fresh, while a new biome raises the player level cap to 50 and equipment cap to 55. 

GeForce NOW offers Enshrouded 1.0 ready to play in the cloud at launch across supported devices. Skip the 60GB local install to save precious storage space, then step into the Shroud without waiting for downloads or needing to make room for the update.

Let the Bolts Fly

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is now streaming on GeForce NOW. The brutal, fast-paced sequel to the retro first-person shooter brings more enemies, more weapons and new ways to purge.

Picking up directly after the original game, a branching single-player campaign sends the fight to grimdark new worlds.

Choose between the formidable Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo and the swift Sister of Battle Nyra Veyrath, each with distinct abilities, weapons and play styles. From towering hive cities to jungle mangrove swamps, new enemy types await in every biome.

GeForce NOW keeps the campaign ready in the cloud. No local rig upgrades or game installs stand between members and the fight — the Emperor’s work waits for no loading bar.

Also this week, the performance of DLSS 5’s 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model is improving by 2X, enabling even more gamers to enjoy DLSS 5’s transformative uplift in lighting and materials at high frame rates and settings. The new, more performant DLSS 5 model will debut in NBA 2K27 on Oct. 16 on GeForce NOW, GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs and RTX Spark laptops.

Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.

items.title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
items.summary: Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation.  But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: […]
items.content:
Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation. 

But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both. 

At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community. 

Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements


NVIDIA is joining the campaign, providing:

  • Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms
  • Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources
  • Skills, training and technical support
  • Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent
  • Support for startups and ecosystem development

“Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.”

Open Models

NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology. 

NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub.

Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit, NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences. 

Skills and Training 

Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute. 

The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline. 

Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs.

Access to Compute

NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France, Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services. 

The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education. 

AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results.

The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe.

Sweden AI Factory, one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. 

Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets.

As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing, the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre, the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY.

AI Infrastructure Expansion

To top it all off, NVIDIA is powering Europe’s most ambitious expansion of AI infrastructure to date, with 35 supercomputers currently in development across the continent — the largest single-year buildout of supercomputing capacity Europe has ever seen.

Together, these systems will equip over 3 million researchers with next-generation infrastructure, accelerating discovery across domains from climate science and drug development to materials research and beyond.

Explore NVIDIA technologies for science and open source courseware, and find hands-on training through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute. 

Follow the European Commission’s RAISE Pledging Initiative.

Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements
