Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI
items.summary:
Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This [...]

Read More...

The post Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM): Scaling the Central Model and Compute Engine for Frontier Ads AI appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
Last year, we introduced GEM, the industry’s largest recommendation system (RecSys) foundation model. GEM established Meta’s first LLM-inspired paradigm for ads recommendation, driving major performance gains. Building on this foundation, our next goal is to further scale both compute and intelligence transfer with next-generation hardware, and expand this capability across Meta’s entire ads ecosystem. This spans dozens of surfaces and objectives, delivering seamless full-funnel optimization across awareness, consideration, and conversions. 

The 2026 generation of GEM shifts from isolated per-domain optimizations — such as Facebook, Instagram, Reels — to a single central foundation model. It learns from data and signals across all of Meta’s ads platforms, bends the scaling curve at LLM-scale computation, and delivers strong advertiser outcomes through post-training techniques that provide a larger latency budget without requiring real-time evaluation of all ad candidates — all on a substantially more efficient training stack. The result is simultaneous ad performance gains across every surface and funnel stage, and deeper understanding that better matches ads to what people are looking for.

GEM has delivered 18.9% conversion improvement and 12% ad click-through rate (CTR) improvement across Meta’s ad surfaces and objectives, and additionally contributed 5.8%, 4.1%, and 1.6% conversion uplift on Facebook, Instagram, and off-site conversion for targeted users over the past year. These gains span both upper-funnel surfaces and deep-funnel optimization goals, driving stronger returns for advertisers.

GEM advances the frontier of recommender systems in the following four areas:

1. Bending the Scaling Curve, Enabling 2.5x Model Complexity 

Challenge: Empirical scaling laws demonstrate that model performance predictably improves with compute, parameter, and data size using transformer model architecture. However, recommender system models do not exhibit similar scaling properties with transformer due to massive heterogeneous features and shifting distributions. 

Solution: We built an LLM-style architecture — Kunlun, co-designed with the latest GPU hardware, to make larger, deeper models substantially more cost-efficient and to enable long-context learning over user engagement history. We observed an LLM-like scaling law at our largest pre-training scale with 2.5x model complexity growth from earlier versions of GEM. The pattern mirrors frontier LLMs: more capacity and longer context produce emergent gains in ranking quality that translate directly into business results.

2. Efficient Intelligence Transfer From GEM to User-Facing Models

Challenge: Serving a model at this scale in real time is prohibitively expensive and drives up latency, compromising both user experience and advertiser ROI. 

Solution: The structured representation, LoopFM, a state-of-the-art post-training technique, transfers GEM’s internal representations and sequential historical memory to downstream models. Through computation sharing, it doubles the intelligence transfer together with the knowledge distillation deployed in the previous version, at no additional compute cost or latency. We also introduced elastic pre-computation (Solaris) to harvest the gains from the upstream model.

3. Accelerating the Central Compute Engine With Large-Scale Cross-Surface, Cross-Domain Learning at Meta Ads Scale

Challenge: Meta’s apps span dozens of surfaces — Facebook, Instagram, Reels, Stories, and more — with 3.6 billion people using at least one of our apps each day. Each surface and optimization objective previously had its own independent prediction system. As the platform grows in surfaces and objectives, so does the challenge of improving ad performance simultaneously.

Solution: GEM accelerates one single, unified compute engine through the central foundation model that jointly predicts clicks and conversions across all surfaces, including Facebook and Instagram, and across every key advertiser objective from off-site conversions to mobile app installs. The generalizable representations learned on data-rich click tasks transfer into data-sparse conversion tasks. A new training recipe with cost-free data mixing and the domain expert framework makes this heterogeneous, large-scale learning tractable, with predictable scale and enhanced reliability.

4. Scaling Total Training FLOPs by 4x While Doubling E2E Training Efficiency Across Thousands of GPUs

Challenge: Training a RecSys foundation model across thousands of GPUs at this scale requires careful orchestration of compute, parallelism, communication, and memory. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization while scale. 

Solution: We developed custom kernels with low precision and new 5D parallelism strategies co-designed with the latest GPU hardware and Meta’s training cluster, and optimized model architecture with infrastructure together to scale efficiently across thousands of GPUs. End-to-end training efficiency is doubled to 20-25% model FLOPS utilization (MFU) with 4x total training FLOPs, enabling GEM to train at LLM-scale at Meta (see full technical story in our companion blog on Training GEM at LLM Scale).

Scaling Law: Bend Scaling Curve at Frontier Scale with Kunlun

GEM introduces a new LLM-style model architecture — Kunlun. Compared to the previous version (Interformer), Kunlun delivers 2x performance gains with the same computation scaling. Kunlun is designed around the following innovations:

  • Standardize and unify architecture framework by seamlessly interleaving lifelong sequence modeling with scalable recommendation-specific cross-interaction. 
  • Introduce scalable architecture through deep co-design with the latest generation of hardware, and computation reduction with almost no model quality regression.
  • Innovate efficient sequence scaling to process longer user engagement contexts with offline sequence infrastructure.

Efficient Architecture for Scaling Recommendations 

GEM’s Kunlun architecture effectively bends the recommender system scaling curve at frontier training scales by empowering ultra-long user sequences and massive user-item interaction features. For the following technical discussion, we define two types of features: non-sequence features (such as user demographics, ad content representations), and sequence features with a sequence of events, each composed of a set of features. 

This architecture introduces three fundamental advancements:

1. A Standardized and Unified Architecture Framework

We advanced the LLM-style architecture to better capture the unique characteristics of recommender system models — specifically, heterogeneous features and data dynamics. 

Each layer consists of:

  • Attention: customize the attention and feed-forward networks to capture the long dependency pattern in user behavior by adapting to data dynamics. 
  • Summarization Component: simplify and enhance the summarization architecture to extract critical user insights from sequences, effectively bridging sequence and non-sequence structure. 
  • Cross Interaction: expand to the mixture-of-experts (MoE) style design, enabling large-scale modeling of complex interactions between sequence and non-sequence features.

2. Introducing Scalable Architecture Through Deep Co-design

We co-designed the architecture with the latest generation of hardware to allow it to grow deeper and wider efficiently:

  • Computation Complexity Reduction via Block Attention: Replacing full self-attention with block-aligned sparse attention reduces the complexity associated with sequence length from quadratic to linear relative to window size, and uses only the window size that is a multiple of block size, friendly for the kernel without partial block size.
  • Component Unification via Architecture Reformulation: Per-Example Feed-Forward Networks (pFFN) was introduced to adapt the traditional FFN to per-example distribution. We reformulated the pFFN component into attention operations through Generalized Dot-Product Attention (GDPA), speeding up training by targeting at unifying the model’s many attention-like operations into a single GPU kernel, delivering up to 2x forward speedup.
  • Scalable Cross interaction through Expert Parallelism: Our cross-interaction component utilizes a scalable, MoE-like framework that employs model-expert parallelism, allowing each GPU to process a subset of expert sub-networks in parallel.

3. Innovating Efficient Sequence Scaling

We introduced specialized component designs to make ultra-long sequences computationally tractable:

Component Skip Connection (CompSkip): The computational skip mechanism selectively activates sequence modules in each layer, and only routes outputs through residual connections. By selectively deactivating the specific components, which is based on the assumption that the network can recover quickly after re-activating, we reduce FLOPS by 43% with negligible quality loss.

Sequence Unification (OneSeq): We selectively unify user sequences chronologically after the event feature aggregation. This allows a single, unified sequence layer to process long sequences, even when individual events possess heterogeneous structures and features. In the system, we have different user sequence sources, some of which have different events features. For example, an event in a purchase sequence can be described by ad ID and account ID, while the event in a post sequence is described by actors and object ID. They cannot simply be unified from the data source level due to the different set of event features. It requires the flexible sequence unification approach to maximize GPU efficiency because of large-size tensor operations and minimizing operator fragmentation.

The GEM Architecture. On the left is the building block, and right is an illustration of the computation skip mechanism.

How Ultra-Long Sequences Matter

The new architecture makes ultra-long sequences feasible. GEM scaled the long engagement context length by 2x in production, and further enabled the capability of scaling long context to 25x, demonstrating infrastructure capability at frontier scale. Along the way, we discovered:

  • Prediction quality follows a power law with sequence length. The relationship is predictable and consistent across sequence lengths.
  • Larger models benefit disproportionately from longer sequences. This creates a virtuous cycle: scaling compute makes the model bigger, which makes longer sequences more valuable. Scaling sequence length makes the model more accurate, which justifies more compute.
  • The two scaling laws reinforce each other, offering investment directions to bend the overall scaling law curve beyond simply adding compute.

Post-Training: Knowledge Transfer at Scale

The value of the foundation model depends on how effectively its intelligence transfers to the hundreds of vertical models that serve ads in real time. GEM revolutionizes post training for recommendation systems through the structure representation with the deep historical memory from the central brain, achieving 2x of transfer effectiveness beyond knowledge distillation. Furthermore, async computation is introduced to a few domain-specific foundation models to transfer the knowledge to vertical models.

Structure Representation at Scale

Knowledge distillation is effective but limited in bandwidth: downstream models only receive a compressed view of GEM’s intelligence at each training process. To address the limitation, we introduce the precomputed structure representation, such as LoopFM, to understand and compress the central brain from the foundation model into a compact representation, and then structure it with deep historical memory. It enables the downstream models to learn the long context from our central brain. It consists of the following major components across the system: 

  • Understand and Compress Intelligence: We compress the intelligence from GEM into the compact representations, which are summarized from the important layers, and used to comprehensively describe the event (or data) that is processed by the foundation model. 
  • Structure with Deep Historical Memory: We structure its compact representation together with the representations that the foundation model previously generated for the same user into a sequential context window, capturing user intent dynamics across all surfaces and traffic through GEM’s memory.
  • Learn from Long Context Intelligence: Downstream models will learn the structure representation with long historical context through the specialized architecture during both inference and training time.

The representation generation process is precomputed and shared with the computation to generate soft labels of the foundation model for knowledge distillation without additional foundation model cost.

Speculative Precomputation for Fresh Predictions

Solaris keeps knowledge transfer fresher, precomputing the user-ad representation from GEM just before vertical model inference needs it. Evaluating the large-scale model inside a live ad request is not affordable, Solaris moves it in time: It speculatively precomputes foundation model embeddings for the user-ad pairs a future request is likely to need, and delivers them just-in-time on the serving hot path. Downstream models gain access to near-real-time foundation model intelligence without being constrained by the latency. Borrowing the idea of speculative decoding from LLM serving, Solaris works through the following major components across the system:

  • Deliver Fresh Runtime Knowledge: It generates the user-ad embedding directly, giving vertical models real-time, point-to-point knowledge of how a specific user is likely to act on the exact ad candidate. 
  • Speculate Ahead of the Request: As multi-stage ranking narrows a live request down to its top ad candidates, Solaris evaluates those user-ad pairs with the foundation model in asynchronous background jobs. The computation carries no latency budget with elastic capacity while it can capture rich knowledge.
  • Enrich Coverage Hierarchically: When an exact user-ad embedding is unavailable, the system degrades rather than drops. It substitutes an aggregate of the user’s own recent embeddings across the same ad groups, or borrows from behaviorally similar users.

Large-Scale Cross-Domain Optimization: Optimize Across Surfaces and Funnels

We further trained GEM with the ads data at Meta scale, including all-surface data (e.g., Facebook and Instagram Feed and Reels/video) and deep funnel optimization (e.g., off-site conversion, mobile app install). GEM powers the first optimized model that jointly predicts both CTR  across all the surfaces and conversion rate (CVR) across the major optimization goals. Previously, each surface and each prediction objective had its own system. This means learnings from engagement patterns across platforms can more directly be used to understand its conversion behavior (e.g., purchase) across ad surfaces. This positions GEM as the central model and compute engine for ads recommendation across Meta’s advertising surfaces. 

Unlike LLMs with the static data, RecSys models need to deal with data dynamics and freshness as well as the diverse distribution across surfaces and traffic. To overcome the challenge, GEM built the first training recipe for the large-scale cross-surface, cross-domain unification through:

A Cost-Free Data Mixing Strategy: It introduced virtual data loading from different combinations of data pipelines without physically merging data together and incurring additional storage cost. It can flexibly adapt to the current ads ecosystem where the downstream models still train with the specific surface or traffic data. We also design a data mixture mechanism to control the mixture proportions during offline and online training close to the real datastream order received in real time, mitigating instability for domain switch and overmemorization for the recent domain data.

A Domain Expert Framework: A shared expert learns a unified representation across all domains, while domain-specific experts capture surface-specific patterns. Each domain expert benefits from both: the shared cross-domain knowledge and its own specialized knowledge. Experts are built on top of the Kunlun architecture framework.

Training a RecSys Model at LLM-Scale Efficiently

GEM now trains at LLM scale on several thousand of the latest-generation GPUs. Today’s data center GPUs and their software stacks are mostly optimized for LLM workloads, whereas recommendation workloads have a fundamentally different profile due to unique data characteristics and rich user & ads signal interaction patterns that make it extremely difficult to achieve high GPU compute utilization for training a foundational recommendation model of GEM’s size. 

We measure training efficiency through E2E MFU, which decomposes into two factors: E2E MFU = Local MFU (compute efficiency) × Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency). Local MFU (compute efficiency) measures how well a single GPU’s compute units are utilized — how close the workload runs to the hardware roofline. Scaling Ratio (scaling efficiency) measures how much single-GPU performance is retained when distributing across thousands of GPUs. This decomposition matters because it lets us treat compute efficiency and scaling efficiency as related but distinct optimization problems, each with its own dedicated set of techniques. Both must be addressed to maximize end-to-end MFU.

We tackled these challenges through complementary compute efficiency and scaling efficiency innovations:  

  • Compute efficiency: Achieved through a customized recommendation kernel library — Jagged Flash Attention (JFA), GDPA, Block-Attention, etc. — and mixed ultra-low precision training (including MXFP8 attention and MLP) optimized for recommendation workloads, purpose-built to leverage the latest generation GPU architecture.
  • Scaling efficiency: Topology-aware 5D parallelism with Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)-free collectives — 2D FSDP + Expert Parallelism for dense parameters, combined with Fully Sharded 2D Model Parallelism for sparse parameters — co-designed with Meta’s multi-tiered network hierarchy to reduce communication overhead.

The result: We doubled GEM’s E2E training efficiency to 20-25% MFU over the past 12 months while scaling total training FLOPs by 4x. Training a foundation model at the intersection of LLMs and recommendation systems is a co-design problem, not a software problem or a hardware problem alone. This 2x efficiency gain came from carefully considering every layer of the stack for optimization — kernels, precision, parallelism, networking, and memory all had to move together.

For the full technical story, see our companion blog: GEM Training: Train Meta’s LLM-Scale Ads Recommendation Model Efficiently.

The Future of RecSys Foundation Models 

Looking forward, we are excited to extend GEM to learn from all of Meta’s platform data, capturing behavior across organic and ads engagements spanning text, images, and video. We’re building toward LLM-scale long context, giving the model the ability to reason over longer spans of engagement context. This will unlock better ad relevance and help advertisers connect with the right audiences more efficiently.

We will continue to scale GEM on even larger compute clusters, opening new scaling opportunities. We are introducing AI-driven optimizations, such as ecosystem enhancement and architecture co-design, to accelerate future evolutions. These optimizations will iteratively refine model architecture in lockstep with hardware advancements, so that each new generation delivers more intelligence per dollar of compute. We will evolve the post-training paradigm with reasoning capability to transfer more of this intelligence to downstream models, further improving advertiser performance and user experience.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank  Laming Chen, Yasmine Badr, Shali Jiang, Hua Zheng, Boyang Liu, Qianru Li, Zhengyu Zhang, Xiaozhen Xia, Angie Huang, Xiaolong Liu, Dan Chanpuriya, Jason Rudy, Cathy Cui, Kenny Lov, Qiuling Suo, Richard Qiu, Wentao Duan, Habiya Beg, Shuo Chang, Wenlin Chen, Xiaorui Gan, John Bocharov, Santanu Kolay, Rocky Liu, Sandeep Pandey, Matt Steiner, Ernest Wang, Musharaf Sultan, Qian Zhao, Anuj Madan, Tak Yan, Viral Vimawala, Saket Gur, Chonglin Sun, GP Musumeci, Jiyan Yang, Jiayi Xu, Chen Liang, Jerry Peng, Zhaojin Wen, Zhichen Zeng, Qinjin Jia, Qinghai Zhou, Rich Zhu, Feipeng Zhao, Hanbin Zhang, Haowen Lin, Lisang Ding, Kai Wang, James Teng, Bingjie He, Donghyun Kim, Yan Deng, Jingyi Shen, Ivonne Xu, Wei Ling, Wen-Chi Yang, Ayush Bihani, Xin Liu, Zikun Liu, Ping Chen, Wankun Zhu, Xian Chen, Jazlyn Li, Hank Lo, Amit Anand Amlesahwaram, Larry Zhang, Hansey Chen, Song Zhou, Zhehui Zhou, Huaqing Xiong, Jie Zheng, Jack Hsueh, Nikhil Garg, Ritwik Tewari, Purbesh Sahoo, Shuby Mao, ​Fan Yang,​ ​Jae-Woo Choi,​ ​Qi Fan​, Peng Zhong​, Peter Lamar​, Bopa Bovet​, Seunghan Lee​, Robert Tang, Lei Zhang, Xi Liu, Hongtao Yu, Lei Tian, Carmen Au, Jake Siso, Rustam Hashimov, Kevin Tang, Bor-Yiing Su, Jade Nie, Tianshu Peng, Subodh Iyengar, Min Si, Ruilin Chen, Max Leung, Rupert Wu, Mandeep Chadha, Angel Yang, Damian Reeves, Hairong Kuang, Ke Sang, Vibha Sinha, Yuzhen Huang, Enes Palaz, Brian Hansen, Liangbei Xu, Oana Platon, Raghav Boinepalli, Rikin Shah, Balaji Balasubramanian, Santosh Mohan, Hao Yan, Eric Falconer,Jacky Zhou, Yusuo Hu, Justin Yang, Pawel Kadluczka, Anamaya Sullerey, Han Xu, Vivienne Sung, Jiasheng Zhang, Serena Liu, Chenxiao Guan, Qiang Jin, Qin Huang, Sagar Chordia, Mingda Li, Li Yu, Ke Pan, May Wang, Sandor Abad, Sandeep Tiwari, Patrick Phelps, Paolo Massimi, Devashish Shankar and the entire team behind the development and productionization of the largest foundation model in Meta’s ads recommendation system.

items.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
items.summary:
Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.

    Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

    How people use Claude for elections and politics

    Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.1

    Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase.

    This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.2

    Connecting people to trusted sources

    Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works.

    Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.

    Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.

    Measuring and preventing political bias

    When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our political evenhandedness evaluation. Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.

    As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies. The Future of Free Speech, an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the Foundation for American Innovation compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The Collective Intelligence Project surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.

    These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.

    We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.

    How we define misuse

    Our Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we announced last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.

    We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently published a guide to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.

    Testing and strengthening our defenses

    We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) and the McCain Institute, both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.

    Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.

    Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share examples of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.

    What we've found

    Our recent threat intelligence report reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.

    Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.

    Looking ahead

    More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.

    Footnotes

    1. We took a random sample of 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026 and analyzed them in a privacy-preserving way.
    2. This figure was generated from a separate analysis of 250,000 Claude.ai conversations, which were reviewed against our election integrity policy.

items.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
items.summary:
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.

“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”

Supporting responsible AI in Singapore

Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.

“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”

“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”

Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.

We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index, and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.

How Singapore is working with Claude

In our latest Economic Index, Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.

In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.

In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.

Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.

Building with the developer community

This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.

Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.

Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our careers page.

items.title: Search agent traces by behavior with AI Search in LangSmith
items.summary:
• AI Search now enables users to find conversations based on semantic understanding of traces, like "did the user get frustrated?" or "did PII leak?"
  • Describe a behavior in plain language, and a fast decision model reads traces and returns the ones where it happened.
  • LangSmith uses trajectories to normalize traces, reduce context bloat, and deliver query results fast.

Agent traces are large, multimodal, and information-dense. They capture key details such as user inputs, how agents respond, and logic failures. That makes traces uniquely valuable for understanding user behavior and improving agent performance, but traditional data platforms weren’t built for large, unstructured payloads like this.

To make trace data useful, teams need infrastructure that can support the full lifecycle: ingest and store high-volume runs, query traces flexibly, and turn them into views for debugging, product analysis, and operational workflows like annotations. That’s why we built SmithDB, the database purpose-built for trace data in LangSmith, and more recently Custom Apps, which let teams create tailored views on top of their traces.

Today, we’re adding AI Search, a new way to query traces using natural language.

Why we built AI Search

Each trace contains user inputs, agent reasoning, tool calls, and responses, all the information required to understand where agents are performing well and where they fail. Teams using LangSmith often mine their agent traces to discover examples for an eval dataset or conversations for a reviewer in an annotation queue.

However, discovering the right traces can be cumbersome. Questions like "did PII leak?" or "did the user get frustrated?" don't map cleanly to a single trace attribute like tags or metadata, and cannot be answered by full-text search either. They require an understanding of the trace contents. Until now, that meant setting up an evaluator ahead of time or going through traces manually.

That's why we built AI Search. You describe the behavior you're looking for, and LangSmith returns the traces where it happened. This enables you to find needle-in-haystack traces and search for troublesome patterns ad hoc.

What you can search for

You can search for anything that shows up in the content of a trace. You might look for an agent that said it finished a task but didn't, a user who seemed frustrated or pushed back on an answer, a request to a model that leaked PII, or someone trying to cancel their subscription. Product teams can search for "requests for integrations we don't support", "competitor mentioned", or "users confused about onboarding" and see where the product falls short, in users' own words.

AI Search also works alongside the filters you already use, so a search can run only on traces that errored, or only with a specific tag.

How we built it

Why a model reads every trace

Vector search is the usual way to search by meaning instead of exact words. It turns your query and each trace into an embedding, a short list of numbers that captures what the text is about. Then it returns the traces whose embeddings are closest to your query's. That works well for topic search, like finding conversations about billing. But an embedding packs a whole trace into one small vector, and that compression is lossy. Important details related to your query can get lost. A trace where the agent did the work successfully and one where it only said it did can end up with nearly the same embedding. Telling them apart takes a model that reads the actual words of the trace along with your question, so it can reason about what happened.

Until recently, doing that at search time was too slow and too expensive. Fast decision models changed that. They answer one narrow question about an input quickly and cheaply enough to run at scale. AI Search pairs decision model inference with SmithDB, our data layer for agent observability. As traces arrive, SmithDB turns them into trajectories. When you run a search, your filters narrow the candidates, and the decision model checks each remaining trajectory against your description.

Traces are large and come in many formats

Traces come from many sources: the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, LangGraph, the Vercel AI SDK, OpenTelemetry, and more. Each records messages a little differently. Traces also repeat themselves. Agents often re-send the conversation history with every LLM call, so the first message shows up again in every call after it.

SmithDB turns these traces into a trajectory for each session. A trajectory is a distilled view of the agent's work: each message, tool call, and tool result, listed once. SmithDB builds it as traces arrive and puts every supported format into the same shape.

AI Search analyzes trajectories instead of raw traces. Because every format has the same trajectory shape, one search works across agents built on different SDKs. Removing the repeat messages reduces context bloat, so searches run faster. A trajectory also covers the whole session, so if you search for "the user tried to cancel", the model sees what the user asked, what the agent did, and how the conversation ended.

Trajectories are still long

Removing duplicates helps, but agent trajectories are still long. To get a sense of how long, we sampled 150 random conversations from Open SWE, the open source coding agent the LangChain team uses every day. Each task runs in its own sandbox with shell access and can hand work off to subagents, so the conversations get big.

A couple of them ran past a million tokens, even in a sample this small. Searching for a rare behavior means reading through a lot of conversations, so AI Search regularly runs into ones that size and can't read every token.

Most questions don't need all of those tokens, though. Many questions are about what the user asked and how the agent replied. In the median conversation, about 2K of its 72K tokens came from the user's messages and the agent's replies. About 85% was tool output, mostly file reads and shell commands.

💡 Even when a trace runs past a million tokens, many questions about agent behavior can be answered with a few thousand.

‍

Each trajectory gets a fixed token budget, filled in priority order. User messages and the agent's replies to the user go in first. The rest of the budget goes to everything else: intermediate AI messages (the agent's reasoning and tool calls), tool results, and system messages. If the next message only partly fits, it's trimmed to fill the budget, and anything after it is dropped.

Searches have to stay fast at scale

SmithDB is built to ingest and scan large volumes of agent trace data. When you run a search, your structured filters narrow the candidates first. The decision model then checks each remaining trajectory against your description, many in parallel. While the model checks one batch of trajectories, SmithDB is already fetching and preparing the next batch. Matches are streamed back as they're found, so you don't wait for the full scan.

What's next

We're still learning which questions people ask most. The hardest conversations to classify are the ones with subtle differences. Telling "the user gave up" apart from "the user got what they needed and left" can come down to a couple of turns in a long trajectory. We want to see whether a model tuned on traces tells them apart more reliably.

The token budget works well when the answer is found in what the user and agent said. Other questions need different evidence. An agent ignoring a tool error only shows up in the tool results. We're exploring ways to pick context based on the question, and signals that show when the model is unsure, so it can take a second pass with more context.

We'd also like to go past a plain list of matches by grouping similar results or summarizing what they have in common.

Get started

AI Search is in public beta on LangSmith Cloud in the GCP US, EU, and APAC regions, at no additional cost. Org admins can turn it on in settings, and it then shows up on the tracing page. The AI Search docs have the details. Let us know what you search for.

‍

items.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
items.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and […]
items.content:
NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents.

Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16. Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. 

New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: 

  • New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: 
    • Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing.
    • The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. 
    • NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support.
  • Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark:
    • Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more.
    • The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app.
    • NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows.
    • NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport.
  • Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark:
    • Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. 
    • GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark.
    • Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app.
  • Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus:
    • A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta.
    • Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23.
    • The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23.

Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools

AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year.

From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. 

Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark

From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app.

These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC.

After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks.

Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions.

Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills. 

NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant.

Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. 

This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint.

Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw.  

Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents.

The Perfect PAIR

Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR, a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems.

The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. 

PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release. 

Sparking Creativity

RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance.

Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark

Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows. 

In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects.

The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds. 

Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content

Available for download now, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles.

A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app.

RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI

ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video.

 

RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow.

For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading. 

Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction

Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download Blender version 5.3 to get access.

Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time. 

Code, Text and Deploy From RTX Spark

Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype. 

RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud.

Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready

NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing:

  • The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm.
  • The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm, with Python 3.15.
  • The first native Conda installer for Windows on Arm, with over 2,000 Conda packages.
  • 97% of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready, thanks to work with the ecosystem. NVIDIA will be working closely with the community to ready the remaining wheels.

Development is now mostly done by agents. NVIDIA Skills — an open source GitHub repository that teaches agents how to use NVIDIA CUDA-X tools and libraries — lets users develop apps that are accelerated on NVIDIA technologies, even without knowing anything about CUDA.

Coding Agents Are Ready for Local AI

In addition to GitHub Copilot — one of the most popular coding agents, used by millions worldwide — adding support for MXC, it’s updating its model router HydraFusion with support for local models. This enables developers to use their local hardware to reduce token consumption while tapping into frontier intelligence.

Microsoft is making coding models, such as MAI 1.1 Coding Flash, available locally, and adding llama.cpp as a backend to Windows ML — extending the supported models and enabling the latest NVIDIA performance optimizations.

Get started with GitHub Copilot running locally when RTX Spark launches.

Llama.cpp Adds Support for Decision Models, Releases a Windows App

Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs.

Llama.cpp is also releasing today Llama Windows, a Windows-native companion app for llama.cpp, enabling an easy-to-use user interface to download and run models locally, without having to go into the command line. This app, like llama.cpp, is optimized for RTX Spark. Learn more on the Hugging Face blog.

Game On: RTX Spark Launches With Hundreds of Top Games and DLSS 5

RTX Spark is ready for gaming, with hundreds of top titles available when laptops launch on Friday, Oct. 16, including CONTROL Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077, Fortnite, Gears of War: E-Day, Genshin Impact, Hogwarts Legacy, Honkai: Star Rail, Marvel Rivals, NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, NBA 2K27, World of Warcraft and many more.

NVIDIA has worked to bring the full stack of RTX technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, Remix, G-SYNC and ray tracing, to the new platform, along with collaborating with game developers to enable anti-cheat support for popular multiplayer games. Learn more about gaming on RTX Spark. 

DLSS 5 Brings Neural Rendering to RTX Spark

NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is also coming to RTX Spark on launch day. The technology uses AI to enhance lighting and materials with lifelike detail, making game worlds and characters more realistic while preserving developers’ artistic vision. A new, 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model debuts in NBA 2K27 on Friday, Oct. 16, boosting frame rates by up to 1.4x. The faster model will also power DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy starting Thursday, Nov. 5, and Where Winds Meet in late November.

DLSS 5 is also coming to NVIDIA RTX Remix on Friday, Oct. 23, so modders can add better materials, lighting and shadows to classic characters and environments, as shown from modder Sparkles/Kim2091 in her in-development project, Fallout 4 RTX.

Read more about DLSS 5 on RTX Spark on GeForce.com.

Game Agents Running Locally on RTX Spark

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is the third-generation SLM for NVIDIA ACE, the suite of technologies for building in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences. The first-generation model was in a public beta earlier this year for PUBG, allowing players to team up with AI teammates, while the more efficient second-generation model previewed in Aniimo at Gamescom, turning standard creatures into voice-responsive companions.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B combines natural conversation with multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding in application state to power fast local voice and device assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces.

Designed for a low memory footprint and fast time to first token, this model enables responsive local experiences while leaving headroom for applications and other AI models. Its new conversational mode helps keep responses concise and speech-ready, and developers can turn reasoning on or off as needed. 

Starting Friday, Oct. 23, test drive the third-generation Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB inside SkyrimNET, an AI nonplayable character (NPC) modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character equipped with personal memory, voice and autonomy for dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly.

Now compatible with RTX Spark, SkyrimNET supports both cloud and local inference across multiple models, with the latest Nemotron models delivering best-in-class performance for efficient and fast in-game interactions. Download the build on GitHub.

Accelerating Modding Workflows in RTX Remix

As AI agents continue to help modders make their favorite classic games compatible with the RTX Remix renderer, NVIDIA is streamlining asset updates with a major overhaul to its AI-powered texture generation workflow. Launching Friday, Oct. 23, as part of Remix 1.6, ComfyUI Version 2 replaces complex REST application programming interface (API) node connections with a dedicated AI tools layout directly in the sidebar.

This update allows modders and artists to generate physically based rendering materials natively inside RTX Remix with zero API setup required. A new batch processing feature makes it easy to scale beyond single-texture experimentation to full modding projects, while an intuitive presets system lets non-technical creators adjust key settings without touching the node graph. 

Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.
