items.title: Building Long-Running Agents with ScaleDown and Deep Agents
items.summary:
• Building long-running agents takes constant context management, and making those decisions with a frontier LLM is slow and expensive. ScaleDown’s constrained decoding models (CDMs) make them faster and cheaper.
  • langchain-scaledown makes it easy to use ScaleDown models in your agent, and ships with middleware for summarization, tool result compression, and extraction.
  • ScaleDown is now supported in the LangSmith LLM Gateway, so its calls are traced and count toward your spend and rate limits.

Building long-running agents comes down to the art of context management: deciding which information goes into the context window, and when. That means summarizing old history, compacting large tool results, and extracting the right data from long inputs. Each of those steps is a decision. Historically we’ve made them with LLMs, which is slow and expensive at the volume a long-running agent needs.

To make those decisions faster and cheaper, we now have a langchain-scaledown integration and support in the LangSmith LLM Gateway for ScaleDown’s constrained decoding models (CDMs). Where a general-purpose LLM writes any string one token at a time, a CDM is trained for one task and only returns answers that task allows, like a label from your list or spans of the input. That lets it be much smaller, faster, and cheaper: ScaleDown reports its models are 200x faster and 467x cheaper than frontier models on these narrow tasks.

The integration ships with three middlewares for LangChain and Deep Agents: one summarizes old history, one compresses large tool results, and one extracts structured data from the conversation. In this post, we cover what ScaleDown’s models are and how to use them to scale down your agent’s context.

What models does ScaleDown offer?

ScaleDown has four models, each trained for a single task, so each can be far more efficient than a general-purpose LLM:

  • Summarize writes a short summary of long text.
  • Compress cuts a block of context down to the parts relevant to a question.
  • Extract pulls the fields you describe out of text, each with a confidence score and its position in the source.
  • Classify scores text against labels you define and returns a probability for each. You can decide whether to return a natural language reason for why the classification was made.

Every model takes up to 1M tokens of input, so a full contract, a long policy page, or an hour of agent history fits in one call with no chunking. They’re also multimodal: Extract, Summarize, and Classify take images and scanned PDFs directly in addition to unstructured text, so a screenshot or a scanned invoice works as an input.

On ScaleDown's own benchmarks, measured against the average of GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini, and GPT-5.4 Nano on public datasets, Summarize is 41x cheaper and 2.7x faster, and Compress is 138x cheaper and 1.8x faster, while scoring higher on accuracy for both.

If you’ve used a decision model like Jev, ScaleDown Classify will feel familiar: both return a typed answer with a probability. Jev takes text only, up to 32K tokens of state per question. Classify takes up to 1M tokens, images included, and adds a one-sentence reason to each decision. When an agent routes a ticket or stops a run based on a label, the reason tells you why, which makes the agent easier to debug.

Summarizing message history

Long-running agents need summarization because their history eventually outgrows the context window. A coding agent that has been working for an hour has dozens of file reads and tool outputs in its history, most of which it no longer needs verbatim. Summarizing them with another frontier model call adds cost and latency every time the history fills up.

ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware replaces Deep Agents’ built-in summarization middleware. It takes the same trigger and keep options to decide when to summarize and which recent messages to keep, and ScaleDown writes the summary:

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware

agent = create_deep_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-6-sol",
    tools=[run_tests],
    middleware=[
        ScaledownSummarizationMiddleware(
            "openai:gpt-6-sol",  # the agent’s model, used for its context window
            trigger=("fraction", 0.8),
            keep=("fraction", 0.1),
        ),
    ],
)

The agent keeps its own model for planning and writing code. Only the summary moves to ScaleDown, which by default returns the same sections as LangChain’s summary prompt (intent, summary, artifacts, and next steps). If a ScaleDown call fails, the middleware leaves history as is and the agent keeps running. The same middleware works with LangChain’s create_agent.

Compressing tool results

Long-running agents call a lot of tools, and every large result stays in context for the rest of the run. A fetched web page can run to tens of thousands of characters when the agent only needs one paragraph of it. Every later step pays for those tokens again, and the agent gets worse at staying on task as its context fills up.

ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware adds an optional compression_query parameter to your tools. When the model only needs part of a result, it fills in compression_query on the tool call, for example "refund policy for EU orders". The middleware strips it before the tool runs, then ScaleDown compresses the output to the relevant parts before the model sees it:

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware

agent = create_deep_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-6-luna",
    tools=[search_docs, fetch_url],
    middleware=[ScaledownToolCompressionMiddleware(tools=["fetch_url"])],
)

Your tools don’t change, so this works with any tool, including MCP tools. In this trace, ScaleDown cut a long docs page by almost 90% before the model saw it. The compressed result starts with a note like this one, so the model can call the tool again without compression_query if it needs the full page:

[Compressed by ScaleDown for "refund policy for EU orders":
 18,402 -> 3,110 chars.
 Call this tool again without `compression_query` for the full output.]

Extracting structured data

Agents constantly pull specific values out of what they read, like an ID, a date, or a field the next tool call needs. That extraction sits inside the agent loop, so it has to be fast enough not to add latency to every turn, and exact enough that a tool can use the value as is.

For example, before a support agent can file a ticket, it needs the order number, the error message, and the customer’s email. The main model could fill those in as tool arguments, but it may paraphrase an error code or mistype an email address instead of copying it exactly.

ScaledownExtractionMiddleware hands this step to ScaleDown. You describe each field in plain language, and Extract copies the value from the text. A field can also be a set of labels, which ScaleDown answers with Classify, so the ticket can be routed by issue type. Before the first model call of a run, the middleware sends the user’s messages to Extract and saves the fields to agent state under scaledown_extraction, where your tools can read them:

from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain.tools import ToolRuntime, tool
from langchain_scaledown import ScaledownExtractionMiddleware

ticket = ScaledownExtractionMiddleware(
    entities={
        "order_id": "Order number the customer mentions",
        "error_message": "Exact error message or code the customer saw",
        "customer_email": "Customer's email address",
        "issue_type": {
            "labels": [
                {"name": "billing", "rubric": "Is this about a charge, refund, or payment?"},
                {"name": "technical", "rubric": "Is this about a bug or something not working?"},
                {"name": "account", "rubric": "Is this about login, password, or account settings?"},
            ]
        },
    },
    context_chars=0,  # skip evidence snippets to keep state small
)


@tool
def file_ticket(runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str:
    """File a support ticket with the details gathered so far."""
    fields = runtime.state.get("scaledown_extraction", {}).get("fields", {})
    return crm.create_ticket(**fields)  # your ticketing system


agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[file_ticket], middleware=[ticket])

Extract only reads the user’s messages, never the agent’s replies, so every value is something the customer actually said. With a checkpointer, extraction re-runs each turn, so the record fills in as the customer adds detail. For "Order A-1042 failed with ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED. I already tried a different card.", the fields come back as:

{
    "order_id": "A-1042",
    "error_message": "ERR_PAYMENT_DECLINED",
    "customer_email": None,  # not mentioned yet
    "issue_type": "billing",
}

Classifying drift

An agent decides its next step based on its current state, like whether the task is done or whether the last tool call worked. Classifying that state happens on every turn, so it needs to be cheap and fast.

One state worth catching in long-running agents is drift: looping on the same failing tool call, or getting stuck in an unproductive cycle. There’s no prebuilt middleware for this, but you can call any ScaleDown model from your own custom middleware. Here’s a circuit breaker that runs after every model call, sends the history to ScaleDown Classify, and stops the run when it’s off track:

import os

import requests
from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import after_model
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, get_buffer_string

LABELS = [
    {"name": "progressing", "rubric": "Is the agent making new progress on the user's task?"},
    {"name": "looping", "rubric": "Is the agent repeating the same steps without new results?"},
    {"name": "drifting", "rubric": "Is the agent working on something the user did not ask for?"},
]


@after_model(can_jump_to=["end"])
def circuit_breaker(state, runtime):
    result = requests.post(
        "https://api.scaledown.xyz/classify",
        headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["SCALEDOWN_API_KEY"]},
        json={"text": get_buffer_string(state["messages"]), "labels": LABELS},
    ).json()

    label = result["top_label"]
    if label != "progressing" and result["scores"][label] > 0.8:
        return {"jump_to": "end", "messages": [AIMessage(f"Stopped: {result['reasoning']}")]}
    return None


agent = create_deep_agent(model="openai:gpt-6-sol", tools=[run_tests], middleware=[circuit_breaker])

Classify returns a probability for each label, so you choose how confident it has to be before the breaker trips. Its one-line reason shows up in the final message, so you can see why the run stopped. A gentler version doesn’t end the run on the first trip: it adds the reason to the conversation as a nudge to change course, and only stops if the agent drifts again.

These four sections show a few places ScaleDown’s models fit, and the list isn’t exhaustive. You can mix and match them, like running extract / summarize on long tool results, or classification for runtime model routing. Check out ScaleDown Cookbooks to see other ways to use CDMs models across different types of data.

ScaleDown in the LangSmith LLM Gateway

The LangSmith LLM Gateway lets you call models across providers with one LangSmith API key, traces every call, and enforces your spend and rate limits. ScaleDown is now one of its direct model access providers, at the /scaledown path.

An admin adds your ScaleDown key to the workspace’s provider secrets as SCALEDOWN_API_KEY once. Then point langchain-scaledown at the gateway and authenticate with your LangSmith key:

export SCALEDOWN_BASE_URL="https://gateway.smith.langchain.com/scaledown"
export SCALEDOWN_API_KEY="$LANGSMITH_API_KEY"

Each ScaleDown call then shows up as a LangSmith trace and counts toward the same limits as your other model calls.

When not to use ScaleDown

Keep a general-purpose LLM for open-ended generation, like writing code, drafting replies, and planning. This follows the "cheap by default, frontier on exception" approach from our Jev posts: use a large general-purpose LLM for the hard parts, and specialized models for the high-volume steps around it.

ScaleDown is fast and cheap enough to run on every turn, so your agent can make the structured decisions that context management depends on without slowing down the main loop or paying frontier prices for them. In a long-running agent, those decisions happen on almost every turn, so the savings add up fast.

Get started

Install the integration and set your ScaleDown API key:

uv pip install -U langchain-scaledown
export SCALEDOWN_API_KEY="..."

New ScaleDown accounts get 50M free tokens. The ScaleDown integration docs cover the configuration options for each middleware. Give langchain-scaledown a try, and let us know what you think on the LangChain forum, X, or GitHub.
items.author: Sydney Runkle, Srimanth Tangedipalli, Neal Patel

items.title: MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads---information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.
items.author: Junlin Chen, Wenhao Wang, Junchao Xu, Qingsong Yao, Fei Xue, Li Sun, Xiao Wang, Ruijie Wang

items.title: HGRP: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Routability Prediction
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Routability prediction enables rapid evaluation of placement quality without routing, providing effective feedback for routability-driven placement optimization. Recent machine learning methods have achieved efficient routability prediction through data-driven approach. However, their prediction performance highly depends on the capability of input representations to capture essential circuit information. To address the limitations of existing circuit representations in simultaneously preserving logical topology, physical layout and routing resource information, this paper proposes HGRP, a heterogeneous graph neural network for routability prediction. HGRP models the cells, nets, and routing grids as distinct types of nodes and explicitly represents topological connectivity, spatial mapping, and grid adjacency, thereby constructing a heterogeneous graph representation that preserves multi-level circuit semantics. Based on the representation, a heterogeneous message passing mechanism is developed to enable information interaction and feature fusion among distinct types of nodes, effectively learning the complex correlations between circuit structures and routing behaviors. Experimental results on the CircuitNet dataset show that HGRP improves F1-score by 18.69\% relative improvements compared with the state-of-the-art in the congestion prediction task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShenShan123/HGPR.
items.author: Yule Sheng, Yue Yuan, Shan Shen, Daying Sun

items.title: Dimension-Optimal Dynamic Regret in Exp-Concave Online Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20187v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tracking changing comparators is a central problem in online learning. For exp-concave losses, previous work established the $T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon $T$ and Euclidean path length $P_T$ for fixed dimension, while the optimal cost of dimension remained unresolved. We resolve this question by establishing a sharp $d^{1/3}$ curved dimension factor, improving the $d^{2/3}$ factor of recent switching and interval reductions [1, 2]. To achieve this improvement, we develop a proper, full-information learner on compact convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that adapts to the unknown path length and, under fixed dimension-independent diameter, gradient, and curvature parameters, guarantees
  $$\operatorname{Reg}_T(u_{1:T}) \le \widetilde{O}\left(d+\min\left\{d^{1/3}T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3},\sqrt{TP_T},T\right\}\right).$$
  A matching lower bound on a diameter-one Euclidean ball establishes the minimax frontier up to logarithmic factors when $T\gtrsim d^2$, including the transition from the curved rate to larger path budgets. The lower bound already holds for losses that depend on only one coordinate per round, isolating an unavoidable cost of learning across directions. Our upper bound follows from square-root Gaussian KL control of comparator movement and a cancellation argument that pays for history restarts. The curved learner maintains $O(\log^2 T)$ Gaussian states, uses one gradient per round, and runs in time near-linear in $T$ under a Mahalanobis-projection oracle.
items.author: Yanyi Li, Wendao Wu, Haihan Zhang, Qinshi Wang, Chenheng Zhang, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin

items.title: RM-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Generative Reward Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning on Mixed-domain preference data (Mix-RL) has become the mainstream approach for training general-purpose Generative Reward Models (GRMs). However, Mix-RL suffers from two critical bottlenecks: the reward sparsity induced by outcome rewards, and the cross-domain interference arising from jointly optimizing heterogeneous capabilities, which together give rise to imbalanced capability acquisition and pervasive reward hacking. Inspired by the success of On-Policy Distillation (OPD) in multi-domain capability integration, we introduce RM-OPD (Reward Modeling via On-Policy Distillation), a two-stage framework that separates specialist acquisition from capability integration. First, we cultivate domain-specialized teacher models via single-domain GRPO fine-tuning, allowing each expert to reach its performance ceiling in isolation; then we consolidate these teachers into one student model through (i) routed on-policy distillation, which provides dense signed token-level supervision on student-generated critiques; (ii) domain contribution reweighting, which reweights token guidance toward target domain shares, preventing specific domains from dominating optimization; and (iii) optional criteria context distillation, which conditions teachers on domain-specific evaluation criteria to sharpen token-level supervision. Across multiple RM benchmarks and two base models, RM-OPD consistently outperforms vanilla Mix-RL and other strong baselines, achieving overall superior performance and exhibiting an emergent "teacher-surpassing" effect. These results establish RM-OPD as a promising paradigm for building generalist GRMs.
items.author: Qinglin Su, Licheng Pan, Zhen Fang, Jiakang Wang, Qingnan Ren, Yunsheng Lu, Yan Gao, Zhixuan Chu

items.title: Optimizing Sparse Boolean Rule Networks using Mixed Integer Linear Programming
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the problem of learning accurate and cognitively simple binary classifiers that are directly interpretable as Boolean rules. We propose mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulations for training sparse disjunctive normal form (DNF) networks, viewed as small networks with a conjunctive hidden layer and a disjunctive output layer. Contrary to previous work that uses MILP for inductive rule learning, we start with a fixed network structure, for which we then find optimal weights. A regularized objective explicitly trades off misclassification costs against sparsity, yielding globally optimized rule sets. Our main technical contribution is an enhanced formulation that substantially reduces the number of integer decision variables and eliminates redundant constraints, while preserving exact Boolean semantics for all feasible solutions. Furthermore, we develop a combined approach based on initialization and dropout to break symmetries in the weights between rules, mitigating redundancy, and encouraging more diverse and stable rule representations. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and UCI datasets show that the advanced formulation improves computational efficiency and achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to established interpretable baselines, including SAT-based DNF learning and well-known rule- and tree-based learners. Overall, our approach provides a principled optimization framework for learning compact Boolean rule sets with explicit control over accuracy and sparsity trade-offs.
items.author: Thomas Pammer, Johannes F\"urnkranz, Markus Sinnl

items.title: In-Context Batch Black-box Optimization via Flow Matching
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Batch black-box optimization is important for expensive systems where many candidates can be evaluated in parallel, yet only a few rounds of evaluation are affordable. In this regime, effective batch construction must identify multiple promising regions while avoiding redundant evaluations, and conventional Bayesian optimization can require increasingly difficult batch-selection procedures as the batch size grows. We introduce Flow Matching for Thompson-Sampling Refinement (FMTR), an amortized approach that learns offline a continuous, history-conditioned proposal distribution from which variable-size batches can be sampled. FMTR is trained offline by conditional flow matching on Thompson-sampling argmaxes refined toward high-value regions via a horizon-dependent Langevin pushforward map, adapting the exploration-exploitation tradeoff over the optimization horizon. At test time, the model parameters remain fixed and batch generation requires neither task-specific surrogate refitting nor numerical acquisition optimization. FMTR achieves strong performance against batch BO and in-context baselines on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, while substantially reducing the computational cost of batch selection.
items.author: Quoc-Anh Hoang Nguyen, Xinyu Zhang, Daolang Huang, Julien Martinelli, Samuel Kaski

items.title: Seeing at the Edge: Energy Characterization of Vision-Language Model Inference on Edge Platforms
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.
items.author: Junlin Liao, Harshit Kondle, Di Liu, Zonghua Gu

items.title: A Bregman Proximal Viewpoint on Neural Operators
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.
items.author: Abdel-Rahim Mezidi, Jordan Patracone, Saverio Salzo, Amaury Habrard, Massimiliano Pontil, Remi Emonet, Marc Sebban

items.title: KANLab: TensorFlow Playground for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KANLab is a browser-based visualization tool designed to interactively teach the core concepts of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), forked from the widely successful TensorFlow Playground. To maximize educational clarity, KANLab omits residual connections and learnable scaling parameters found in modern KAN implementations, ensuring that displayed B-spline activation curves directly correspond to their underlying trainable control points. Users can inspect and modify activation functions, initialization schemes and observe gradient descent correcting manual disruptions. Furthermore, user can explore phenomena such as activation variance, interactive pruning, and re\-/training within a compact 2D machine learning setting. KANLab is open-source and available at https://kanlab.app/
items.author: Lukas Niehaus, Robin Rawiel, Ulf Krumnack

items.title: From Spectral to Frobenius: When Muon Loses Its Spectral Implicit Bias
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20112v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior work on implicit bias shows that gradient descent selects the Frobenius max-margin direction on linearly separable problems, whereas Fan et al. (2025) established spectral max-margin behavior for spectral-norm steepest descent methods, including idealized Muon with exact orthogonalization. In practice, however, Muon approximates orthogonalization using finite Newton-Schulz iterations and a positive stabilization constant. We prove that these implementation choices cause Muon to select the Frobenius rather than the spectral max-margin direction in linear classification with separable data. We also establish this behavior for both exponential moving average and Nesterov-style momentum. The key technical ingredient is a summable perturbation argument showing that the resulting parameter trajectories remain at bounded distance from those of gradient descent. We then disentangle the roles of Newton-Schulz iteration count, the stabilization constant, and the Newton-Schulz polynomial, revealing distinct asymptotic behaviors, including directions that achieve neither Frobenius nor spectral max-margin. Finally, we show that Muon can recover its spectral max-margin bias with Newton-Schulz iterations growing logarithmically over training.
items.author: Yongtao Wu, Mahdi Mansouri, Zhenyu Zhu

items.title: Exhaustive Canonical Skeletons Generation: A Formal Dataset for Decomposable Symbolic Regression
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural symbolic regression (SR) models require diverse datasets of mathematical expressions for robust training. However, existing datasets rely predominantly on stochastic sampling methods, which suffer from high structural redundancy and incomplete functional coverage. To address this, we introduce an exhaustive dataset of univariate canonical skeletons generated via a deterministic constrained context-free grammar. A canonical skeleton acts as a generic structural representation that subsumes more specific functional forms, eliminating redundant expressions and avoiding repeated computational efforts. Although our dataset consists of univariate skeletons, it is designed to support the decomposable SR paradigm to solve multivariate SR problems without assuming linear separability. Furthermore, we pair this dataset with a sampling strategy that generates clean numerical data without triggering numerical instabilities or relying on artificial protected operators. Canonicalizing two existing neural SR datasets reveals that our dataset is substantially more compact, eliminates structural repetitions, and achieves a uniform operator distribution free of simplicity bias. Finally, we establish a benchmark of 150 SR problems across three tiers, on which state-of-the-art SR methods are shown to struggle significantly.
items.author: Giorgio Morales, Anik\'o Ek\'art

items.title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.
items.author: Fernando Acero

items.title: A Large-Dimensional Analysis of Least-Squares Federated Learning via Generalized Total Variation Minimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated learning over decentralized networks inherently trades off the suppression of local finite-sample noise through collaboration against the bias that collaboration introduces between heterogeneous nodes. We study this tension by performing a large-dimensional analysis of Generalized Total Variation Minimization with least-squares models. Using tools from random matrix theory, we show that Lipschitz observations of the global GTVMin solution concentrate in large dimensions, universally for any underlying network structure. We provide exact analytic expressions for the asymptotically precise performance under both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. Gaussian mixture distributions on a fixed network. For the latter, these expressions quantify how regularization balances local adaptation against collaboration. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world data.
items.author: Ekkehard Schnoor, Malik Tiomoko, Alexander Jung

items.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.
items.author: Tinglan Wang, Haixu Liu, Shaobo Chen, Nuo Qian, Qi Gao, Kai Wen, Yu Yao

items.title: Trainable at Depth, Solvable at Small Size: What the Loss Surface of a Polynomial Activation Dictates for Designing, Initializing and Training Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: What makes a deep network train, and what shape is its loss surface? We answer both with one construction at two scales: a polynomial activation f (z) = z + {\lambda}z 3 , clamped and projected onto the unit sphere, plus an unnormalized identity path. As a deep stack it trains to one hundred layers on MNIST with no normalization machinery; as a small model its square loss is a polynomial system we solve exactly. The small scale explains the large one: it prescribes how to design, initialize and train the stack.
items.author: Xiuyi Yang

items.title: GBTSVR: Twin Support Vector Regression via Granular Ball Computing
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Regression models used in real-world applications are often challenged by noise, outliers, data heterogeneity, and asymmetric error characteristics, which severely limit the effectiveness of conventional point-wise learning models. While twin support vector regression (TSVR) partially addresses these issues through the use of nonparallel regression bounds, it still relies on individual samples as basic learning units. As a result, TSVR remains highly sensitive to noisy and contaminated observations and fails to leverage the underlying structural and regional information inherent in complex datasets, leading to suboptimal robustness and generalization performance. To address these limitations, we introduce granular ball twin support vector regression (GBTSVR) and its quantile extension, granular ball twin support vector quantile regression (GB-TSVQR). The proposed models integrate granular ball computing with TSVR, replacing individual data points with compact, structure-preserving granular balls as fundamental learning units. This region-level representation effectively suppresses noise and outliers while preserving intrinsic data geometry, thereby enhancing robustness, stability, and generalization. GBTSVR constructs nonparallel lower- and upper-bound regression functions over granular balls, significantly reducing sensitivity to sample-level perturbations. Building upon this framework, GB-TSVQR further incorporates quantile regression principles to simultaneously capture heterogeneous trends and asymmetric error distributions across different quantile levels. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets, time-series benchmarks, and outlier-contaminated data demonstrate that the proposed GBTSVR and GB-TSVQR consistently outperform state-of-the-art regression models.
items.author: A. Quadir, M. Tanveer

items.title: From Earth to Orbit, France’s Ecosystem Delivers Agentic Computing at Scale With NVIDIA
items.summary: Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application.  France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork.  The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments […]
items.content:
Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. 

France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. 

The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack.

Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

 

Sovereign AI Infrastructure

France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. 

Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. 

Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks, a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space, the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit.

Open Models

NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. 

LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement, making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. 

In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA.

Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries.

Fondation Inria, with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year. 

Agents at Work Across Industries

Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France. 

L’Oréal is integrating NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients.

Mirakl has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours.

Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective are demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance. 

Omi helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference.

In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA Cosmos open world models, Nemotron and Omniverse libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses. 

Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos. 

Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care.

In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment

In quantum, Alice & Bob has integrated the NVIDIA NVQLink platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities.

Quandela has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a DGX Spark system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications.

Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

The post OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: 
    • Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube).
    • Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network
    • MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol.
    • Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP.
  • We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure.

At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. 

Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative.

This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone. Here’s some of what’s new:

  • The 102.4T scale-out switch: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters.
  • The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners.
  • Scale-across for multi-site clusters: Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances
  • Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips.
  • Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA): a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP.
  • MetaRoCE: Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations.

The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale

As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack.

IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). 

This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers.

Scaling AI Fabrics From Building to Region

As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible.

Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): More Resilient, Larger Clusters

We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric.

With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages:

  • Larger non-blocking GPU clusters compared to single-plane topologies, which enables the scale required for our largest AI training workloads
  • A flattened topology, moving from the 3-tier Clos fabric of our NSF fabric to a 2-tier Clos fabric. Removing this tier of switches reduces network hops, latency, and infrastructure cost.
  • NIC-level hardware load balancing: Load balancing, traditionally done by network switches, now starts at the NIC, which sprays every packet across all eight planes in hardware.
  • A combined control plane for fault tolerance: The control plane of FPF includes both the switches and the hosts, allowing the host to steer traffic away from downed planes. 

Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings.

Bridging On-Prem Data Centers and Public Cloud

This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure. 

Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit.

That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale.

At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches.

The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work. 

BAG: Scale-Across Aggregation

The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space.

At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement.

Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff. 

We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG.

The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors.

SRv6-Powered Regional Backbone Using FBOSS

We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI.

Ethernet for Scale-Up: Our Commitment to Ethernet

A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies.

Tahan: Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch

We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology.

Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS.

Next-Generation Scale-Up: 72 Accelerators per Rack on 102.4T Silicon

We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack.

ESUN Evolving

The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for:

  • Protocol headers and framing optimized for scale-up topologies.
  • Error handling mechanisms for lossless multi-hop fabrics.
  • Alignment with UEC and IEEE standards.

This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it.

Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases.

With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future.

Ecosystem Enablement and Open Transport

Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols.

OSPA: Open Switch Platform Architecture

SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable.

To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer. 

OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for:

  • Power management and power sequencing.
  • Sensor and environment control, including thermal and fan management.
  • Hardware inventory management and device enumeration.
  • Out-of-band hardware interfaces (management Ethernet, serial console, USB, LED indicators).
  • Firmware maintenance and updates.
  • Platform troubleshooting and diagnostics.

FBOSS Ecosystem Enablement

Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware.

Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository.

MetaRoCE: Open-Source Transport for AI Clusters

As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics. 

At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack.

Join Us in Building the Open Future of AI Networking

The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone.

We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands.

The authors are members of the Network Infrastructure team at Meta.

items.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.
items.author: Samuela Rokocakau, Panagiotis Kakosimos, Giulia Tresca, Pericle Zanchetta

items.title: On the Convergence of Semi-Gradient TD: A Mean Field Perspective
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20014v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semi-gradient temporal-difference learning is a core algorithmic component of reinforcement learning, but bootstrapping with function approximation generally induces a non-conservative vector field and can lead to instability. We analyze this effect for two-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime and identify a simple stability mechanism in which entropy-induced relaxation dominates the sensitivity of the moving bootstrap target. Under this condition, we prove exponential convergence to a unique fixed point and quantify its bias relative to the unregularized Bellman solution. We also show that the same mechanism extends to entropy-regularized off-policy control through soft Q-learning.
items.author: Haruki Settai, Tadashi Kozuno, Shinji Ito

items.title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.20012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.
items.author: Hanyao Guo, Mo Cui, Zihan Tan, Leixin Sun, Yichun Wang, Yinan Shen, Guojun Zhu, Jia Jiang, Erhao Chen, Zui Chen, Wenzhe Gao, Zhihao Yu, Qijun Wang, Yetian Zhu, Jiande Chen, Chuhang Pei, Yao Jiang, Yichen Fan, Pinhan Wang, Xiaorui Pan, Qianyi Zhu, Yang Liu, Mang Ye, Guancheng Wan

items.title: LLM-BabyBench: Can Language Models Plan in Worlds They Can Simulate?
items.summary:
arXiv:2505.12135v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Interactive benchmarks for LLMs usually report a single metric, even though succeeding in them requires models to show several different skills. While those benchmarks are useful for measuring the overall capability of models to perform the downstream task, it is harder to identify which skill was lacking and caused failure solely from the aggregate score. For example, in benchmarks where models are supposed to navigate a simulated world to perform a task, failures can come from perception, an ambiguous instruction, retrieval, missing commonsense about what actions do, unknown dynamics, or planning. \benchmark recasts the procedurally generated BabyAI gridworld as a fully observable, purely textual environment designed to evaluate planning separately from those factors. The nature of the environment and the structure of the prompt control for the other factors cited above. To evaluate the models, we define the PPD suite: \textbf{Predict} asks for the state that follows an action sequence, \textbf{Plan} asks for an action sequence that reaches a goal, and \textbf{Decompose} asks for a subgoal sequence that achieves a mission. Across seven frontier and open models, queried zero-shot, we find simulation far ahead of planning for every model, close to saturated for the strongest. The length of the required solution governs planning failure, and each of the four strongest models has a horizon beyond which single-attempt success collapses. The responses of claude-opus-4-6 and claude-sonnet-4-6, which show their working step by step, reveal that they plan by proposing L-shaped corridors, which is consistent with their successful plans staying near-optimal while success falls. At the subgoal level, decomposition precision likewise falls to zero on long missions, while comprehension of those missions persists.
items.author: Idriss Malek, Omar Choukrani, Daniil Orel, Anh Duy Le Dinh, Zhuohan Xie, Zangir Iklassov, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Salem Lahlou

items.title: Equitable Intelligence in Practice: A Fairness Audit of Open Large Language Models for Library Reference Services
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.18935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As libraries explore large language models (LLMs) as a scalable layer for reference services, a core fairness question follows: can LLM-based services support all patrons fairly, regardless of demographic identity? LLMs could broaden access to information assistance, but they may also reproduce societal biases embedded in their training data and undermine libraries' commitments to impartial service. In this chapter, we apply an evaluation protocol that combines diagnostic classification, which detects systematic differences between responses, with linguistic analysis, which helps interpret them. Across three widely used open models (Llama-3.1 8B, Gemma-2 9B, and Ministral 8B), we find no compelling evidence of systematic differentiation by race/ethnicity, and only minor evidence of sex-linked differentiation in one model and one setting. We discuss implications for equitable AI adoption in libraries and the importance of ongoing monitoring in aligning LLM-based services with social justice goals.
items.author: Haining Wang, Jason Clark, Angelica Pe\~na

items.title: The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.02753v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Python programs pay for their imports at every process start, a cost that is invisible in steady-state benchmarks but dominant for command-line tools, test workers, and serverless cold starts. Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) on largely anecdotal evidence. We measure the import cost of the 500 most-downloaded PyPI packages, every quarterly release since mid-2021, under six CPython versions (3.9-3.14) on two platforms (Apple M5/macOS and Intel Xeon/Linux): all 66,816 package-version-interpreter cells, plus the release histories of 65 distributions beneath shared namespaces, and targeted experiments that isolate individual effects. Import cost is heavily skewed (median 12.3 ms, 99th percentile 400 ms on macOS). For the median package, 68-79% of import time is spent importing the standard library, while third-party dependencies are the largest component in the slowest decile. The cold first import is almost entirely bytecode compilation on Linux, but on macOS 67% of the cold penalty remains when bytecode is precompiled: we trace it to the operating system's security assessment of each new native library, which every fresh environment pays again. A package's own import code grows by a median 4.0-5.0% per year; resolving dependencies as of each release raises the median trend of the total from 1.8% to 3.0-3.4% per year. CPython 3.14 executes package code faster than 3.9 but imports more and slower standard-library modules, a net 1.16x slowdown on macOS and 1.07x on Linux. What dependents actually import from a package costs a median 1.0x its top-level import but 10.9-13.4x at the 90th percentile. Global lazy mode makes import statements essentially free and breaks 10 packages. Harness, analysis code, and dataset are public.
items.author: Trinath Sai Subhash Reddy Pittala

items.title: FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.11308v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability.
  We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,649 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 49 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.91%. This cost-reduction trend holds across different LLM backends and repeated runs.
items.author: Yiming Zhang, Jiangrong Wu, Yuhong Nan

items.title: Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.04058v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to port scientific codes across heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) programming models, such as translating CUDA to OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos or SYCL. However, current evaluations use compilation success, token-level similarity, or developer-written tests from static benchmarks, which cannot reliably ensure behavioral correctness. We present Kaizen, a metamorphic fuzzing and differential testing framework for evaluating the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code. Kaizen uses metamorphic fuzzing via source-code mutation to generate semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing to explore behavioral diversity, and differential testing to expose semantic divergences between original and translated applications that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results. We evaluate Kaizen on CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 scientific applications from seven domains using three fine-tuned LLMs at kernel-level and full-program granularity. Our evaluation reveals that (1) compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; (2) LLM-translated programs exhibit systematic compile-time error patterns, with nine categories for kernel-level translation and 27 for full-program translation; (3) semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose; and (4) full-program translation is substantially harder than kernel-level translation. These findings highlight the need for correctness-oriented evaluation of LLM-assisted HPC code translations.
items.author: Oscar Ludwig, Ninad Anklesaria, Zheming Jin, Swaroop Pophale, Kausar Moshood, Christian J. DeVore, Brandon Gill, Cassius Villareal, Keita Teranishi, Manish Motwani

items.title: WebCQ: Cooperative Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scalable Web GUI Testing
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.22502v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL)-based techniques have shown promise for GUI testing. However, as the complexity of modern GUI software increases, existing MARL-based approaches (e.g., MARG and Fastbot) struggle to scale due to the inherent limitations of their underlying tabular reinforcement learning algorithms. This limits their applicability to large-scale commercial GUI software, especially web applications with vast state spaces and many interactive elements. To fill this gap, we propose WebCQ, a novel MARL-based approach for scalable web GUI testing. WebCQ incorporates QTRAN for multi-agent coordination and a lightweight synchronization mechanism, allowing it to work under asynchronous web testing scenarios. It extracts semantic and exploration features for each UI event to form an action vector. This vector is concatenated with the current state vector and fed into the policy network, enabling DQN-based decision making within a dynamic action space. We evaluated WebCQ on eight large-scale commercial websites. Under the same time budget and agent count, WebCQ explored 33.3% more states and executed 42.2% more unique actions than MARG, while triggering more failures on six of the eight websites under test. It also demonstrated strong scalability, maintaining higher action throughput during 20-hour experiments, and achieving greater performance improvements as the number of agents increased. These results show that WebCQ overcomes key limitations of existing MARL-based approaches, providing a scalable and effective solution to enhance modern web GUI testing.
items.author: Yujia Fan, Sinan Wang, Zebang Fei, Yao Qin, Huaxuan Li, Yepang Liu

items.title: Porting Declarative UI to HarmonyOS: A Heuristic-guided Approach for lightweight LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.07085v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As an emerging operating system, HarmonyOS has a significant demand for software migration, where the User Interface (UI) translation accounts for a critical link. However, recent UI development has shifted to declarative paradigms, e.g., Kotlin Jetpack Compose (KJC) for Android, SwiftUI for iOS, and ArkUI for HarmonyOS, making prior translation approaches inapplicable because they target either backend logic or legacy imperative UIs. Thus, related research is limited.
  To systematically evaluate KJC/SwiftUI-to-ArkUI migration, we build a parallel benchmark of 100 KJC and 100 SwiftUI files across eight scenarios, plus 52 real-world UI pages from nine open-source apps. Evaluating nine direct-translation setups (including diverse LLMs and agents), we find Compilation Success Rate (CSR) spans 0.00%-35.00%; common strategies (reference screenshots and compiler-guided repair) lift capable setups to 94.00%-99.00% CSR but fail on lightweight LLMs. By manually analyzing a 3,102-sample subset, deriving a regular-expression pattern for each failure family, and applying these patterns to generalize the resulting taxonomy to the full 29,593-sample set, we find residual errors rooted in (1) broken structure, (2) nonexistent APIs, and (3) missing resources (e.g., colors, strings, and icons).
  Accordingly, we propose ArkTrans, a declarative UI translation framework that maps these roots to deterministic structure supply, ArkUI knowledge and resource reference injection via a demonstration example, and iterative repair targeting residual errors, via four steps: Metadata Extraction, Skeleton Construction, LLM-driven Translation, and Compiler-Guided Iterative Repair. With Qwen3.6-27B, ArkTrans raises CSR from 0.00% to 70.00% on KJC and 64.00% on SwiftUI, achieving strong visual fidelity, and attains 65.63%/80.00% CSR on real-world pages, far outperforming the best common strategy at lower token cost.
items.author: Kunwu Zheng, Pengyu Xue, Zhen Yang, Tianlong Chen, Xiran Lyu, Peishi Lai, Mengying Zhao, Junjie Chen, Yutian Tang, Huizhi Zhang, Xianhang Li, Linhao Wu, Chengyi Wang

items.title: CUJBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Browser-to-Backend Failure Diagnosis
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.23455v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated failure diagnosis requires correlating browser-visible symptoms with backend observability signals, yet existing benchmarks do not evaluate this cross-modal reasoning task. Constructing one is non-trivial: multi-modal failure scenarios are costly to annotate, and live-environment capture introduces stochasticity that makes cross-run agent comparison unreliable. We present CUJBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark to combine browser-visible failure evidence with backend observability in a diagnostic framing. CUJBench addresses annotation cost through an LLM-assisted generation pipeline with a multi-agent review loop and a three-layer annotation scheme, producing 87 labeled scenarios across five fault families, and ensures reproducibility by packaging each failure as a deterministic multi-modal snapshot with a fixed tool interface. Evaluating six LLMs under retrieval, browser-only, and full-toolset baselines, the benchmark yields an overall accuracy of 21.6% with a ceiling of 52.5%, well below saturation. Contrary to expectation, browser-only agents outperform full-toolset agents in aggregate, with expanded evidence access inducing unfocused exploration rather than improved synthesis. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-modal synthesis as the primary bottleneck: agents retrieve the decisive evidence but fail to attribute it correctly, a failure that persists across all six models and that model scale and richer tool access alone cannot resolve.
items.author: Haoming Meng

items.title: SpecSyn: LLM-based Synthesis and Refinement of Formal Specifications for Real-world Program Verification
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.21570v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Program verification is a formal technique to rigorously ensure the correctness and fault-freeness of software systems. However, constructing comprehensive interprocedural specifications for full verification obligations is time-consuming and labor-intensive, giving rise to automated specification generation approaches. Despite the significant advancements in these approaches brought by Large Language Models (LLMs), existing LLM-empowered approaches still suffer from significant limitations: they lack effective strategies for handling sizable input programs, and are typically equipped with no mechanisms to evaluate and guarantee the strength of the generated specifications. The limitations impair their ability to extract precise specifications from real-world complicated programs to support the verification of target properties, thereby hindering the applicability of existing approaches in verification tasks on real-world programs. To remedy this gap, we propose SpecSyn, a novel LLM-based specification generation method. SpecSyn first decomposes the input program into individual segments, which are handled respectively by the subsequent iterative specification generation process.
